original_title: Spillover Effects: How the Middle East crisis threatens food security - Focus on Myanmar (Date Released: 5 June 2026 / Reporting period: week of 1 June )
title: Spillover Effects: How the Middle East crisis threatens food security - Focus on Myanmar (Date Released: 5 June 2026 / Reporting period: week of 1 June )
original_summary:
Country: Myanmar
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Overview

As of the first week of June 2026, the Iran-US/Israel conflict that began on 28 February remains in a fragile ceasefire. The initial largescale strikes on Iranian military triggered the largest oil supply shock in history, temporarily disrupting 10-20% of global supply and causing significant volatility in energy markets. Higher energy costs are fueling inflation, raising transportation and logistics expenses, and driving up food prices through diesel and fertilizer shortages. The crisis is placing pressure on import-dependent economies. Myanmar ranks among the most severely affected countries in Asia due to its near-total dependence on imported fuel. Dramatic price surges have led to persistent fuel shortages, queues at petrol stations, rationing, and vehicle-use restrictions. These disruptions have hampered commodity flows, weakened market functionality, and eroded household purchasing power. Compounded by fertilizer shortages and existing internal conflict, the situation threatens agricultural production ahead of the monsoon season and further exacerbates food insecurity and humanitarian challenges.

Summary

• Food insecurity: WFP estimates that if the conflict continues through Q2, at least 45 million additional people globally may face acute food insecurity, including over 9 million in Asia. In Myanmar, a further 3.5–5 million people could become food insecure due to this crisis, on top of the existing 12.4 million. The crisis is intensifying vulnerabilities, especially in conflict-affected and remote areas, as reduced agricultural output, rising prices, and market disruptions strain household food consumption and livelihoods.

• Fuel prices: Diesel prices have risen by an average of 68 percent nationwide, with Yangon seeing a 70 percent increase. Octane 95 has increased by 77 percent on average, with extreme spikes in Sittwe (up to tenfold) and Myitkyina (nearly fourfold compared to precrisis Yangon levels). Prices remain high but have gradually declined since late April.

• Food basket cost: As of early June, the average food basket cost is about 19 percent higher than in late February, driven mainly by increases in rice, palm oil, and salt prices.

• Conflict-affected areas: Fuel shortages and price increases of over 70 percent since February have led to queues, rationing, and transport restrictions, delaying the delivery of food, medicine, and aid. Roadblocks and insecurity continue to drive up staple food prices across Kachin, Kayin, Kayah, Sagaing, Rakhine, Magway, and Shan.

• Agriculture: During the monsoon planting season, farmers face fuel shortages and higher fertilizer costs linked to the fuel crisis. These challenges are delaying land preparation, increasing production costs, and limiting market access, raising risks to agricultural output and incomes.

original_title: Middle East Crisis: Risks and Impacts for Food Security in Tanzania (June 2026)
title: Middle East Crisis: Risks and Impacts for Food Security in Tanzania (June 2026)
original_summary:
Country: United Republic of Tanzania
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Key Highlights

ENERGY SHOCK

• Tanzania is highly exposed to external fuel shocks, as it import 100% of fuel. Between 56% and 59% of fuel passes through the Strait of Hormuz.

• Fuel prices remain elevated; petrol up by 47%, diesel up by 60% compared to February 2026.

• LPG price increased by 9% to 17% for 15 kg and 6 kg cylinders, respectively. Tanzania imports 100% of the LPG.

TRADE DISRUPTION

• Higher global energy prices and freight costs increased Tanzania's import bill, especially for capital and industrial goods.

• Imports value increased by 15.5% driven by industrial inputs, machinery and transport equipment.

• Faster import growth than exports widened Tanzania’s current account deficit to about USD 2.65 billion by April 2026.

INPUT CONSTRAINTS

• Prices of some imported fertilizer (SA, DAP and CAN) have increased by 40%, 22% and 11% respectively since the start of the crisis.

• High fertilizer import dependence (80–90%) risks production in upcoming seasons.

MACROECONOMIC STRESS

• Inflation rose to 4.2% in May, driven by energy and transport costs.

• Energy inflation (5.3%) is transmitting into food and logistics sectors.

• Exchange rate remains relatively stable, supported by gold exports.

• Tanzania has sufficient foreign exchange reserves to meet external obligations for four months, although strained by high demand for foreign exchange.

• Prudent central bank actions and adequate liquidity helped smooth volatility and support market order.

original_title: World: Monthly market update #2 – June 2026, Middle East, Northern Africa and Eastern Europe
title: World: Monthly market update #2 – June 2026, Middle East, Northern Africa and Eastern Europe
original_summary:
Countries: World, Egypt, Iran (Islamic Republic of), Türkiye, Yemen
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

HIGHLIGHTS

The temporary reopening of the Strait of Hormuz following a June US–Iran agreement eased global commodity and inflationary pressures, with Brent crude falling 20% in June (compared to May) reaching USD 73/bbl, and urea prices dropping 21% below pre-conflict levels. Cereals and natural gas prices also declined slightly (45%), although natural gas remained 37% above pre-conflict levels.

Annual Inflation remained highly uneven across the region in June, with Iran and Türkiye continuing to face the region’s highest price pressures, while most countries recorded stable or easing inflation and Gaza’s deflation reflected ongoing normalization from conflict-driven price spikes.

Food basket costs were broadly stable in June across most of the region, reflecting easing inflationary pressures; with Iran as a notable exception (+8% MoM, +120% YoY).

Inflationary pressures continue to erode purchasing power of cash transfer values in Iran and Türkiye, constraining vulnerable households’ access to adequate and nutritious food

Most regional currencies remain weaker than pre-escalation levels (February 2026), despite modest June recoveries in some markets, most prominently in Iran (+6%) and Egypt (+4%), while currencies in Armenia, Palestine, and Yemen (IRG) maintained relative stability or strengthening over the past year.

Regional fuel prices eased in June following declining global energy prices and improving geopolitical conditions, with cooking gas and diesel recording the largest month-on-month declines, while generally remaining above pre-conflict levels.
